claims.text: The baseline alloy has composition Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
The baseline alloy is obtained by arc melting.
At melt-spinning cooling rates of approximately 10^5–10^6 K/s, the baseline alloy shows limited amorphous retention and complex crystallization during reheating.
Approximately 1 at% Gd should be added while removing an equivalent amount of a primary element, exemplified by Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni15P20Gd1.
Gd is a large-atom micro-alloying element relative to constituents such as Ni.
Adding approximately 1 at% Gd to the Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni-P alloy will increase atomic-size mismatch and chemical disorder.
The Gd-induced size mismatch will create local stress and packing frustration in the multicomponent matrix.
The additional local stress and packing frustration will disrupt crystal nucleation and growth.
Disruption of nucleation and growth will kinetically hinder crystallization during rapid solidification.
The same mechanism will reduce crystallization during subsequent reheating.
Relative to Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20, the Gd-modified alloy will retain more amorphous material after rapid quenching.
Relative to the baseline, the Gd-modified alloy will have fewer and/or delayed crystallization events in DSC during reheating.
The proposed benefit is expected under rapid solidification by melt-spinning and controlled reheating.
The benefit may be less pronounced under very slow cooling or extreme thermal cycling.
The magnitude of improvement will depend on Gd concentration, distribution, and interactions with the other elements.
Modeling of micro-alloyed Pd-Ni-P found a noticeable effect from Gd at concentrations below 1 at%.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing baseline and approximately 1 at% Gd-modified alloys under identical quenching and reheating conditions using XRD, TEM, DSC, and thermography.
A lack of statistically significant improvement in amorphous retention, or more pronounced crystallization in the Gd-modified alloy, would falsify the hypothesis.
